transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alice Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Shah (GammaHealth ML), Tom Reyes (GammaHealth CTO), Angelica Moreno (GammaHealth PM)

Summary (auto): short demo of Optimize console q-profiles; focus on latency vs quality; pilot ask and security follow-up.

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Alice Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, super excited to walk through the Optimize q-profile flow today. Marcus and I will do a quick run of the console then dig into your EHR summarization tradeoffs.
[00:00:17] Dr. Priya Shah: Hey Alice, thanks. We're mainly concerned about latency for our real time summarization (sub-second for <256 tokens) but also accuracy — medical correctness is non negotiable.
[00:00:30] Alice Park: Yep understood. We'll show INT8 and FP8 profiles and the console's comparison tools. Marcus, want to kick off with the model selection?
[00:00:37] Marcus Li: Sure. So on the Optimize tab I picked model-x-large-v2 as the base, we created two q-profiles — int8-speed and fp8-fidelity. The console shows expected p95 latency and estimated token cost side-by-side. Note these are runtime estimates based on your sequence length distribution.
[00:00:55] Tom Reyes: Quick question — how much of that number is measured vs estimated? We run a lot of short sequences, mean ~120 tokens.
[00:01:03] Marcus Li: Good call. The first column is the emulator estimate. We also have an A/B bench runner that runs a sampled workload for 1k requests to get measured p50/p95. For your short seqs, actual p95 for int8-speed was about 60ms on T4 equivalent in our sandbox, fp8-fidelity about 120ms. But, caveat, your model and longer contexts change that.
[00:01:26] Angelica Moreno: Are those numbers on your hosted infra? We can't send PHI to hosted, so we need private deployment numbers.
[00:01:33] Alice Park: Right — for Private (VPC/on-prem) we provide the same Optimize console but run inside your network; the profiler runs there and reports back aggregated metrics. The kernel/placement differences can shift absolute latencies but relative gaps (int8 ~ 2x faster than fp8) usually hold.
[00:01:51] Dr. Priya Shah: And about quality — do you do automatic evals? We have a clinical QA rubric.
[00:01:58] Marcus Li: The console supports eval sets; you can upload reference pairs and run BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics or custom rubric. We ran a small sensitivity check and saw FP8 preserved clinical detail on 98% of cases while INT8 dropped to 92% on our sample — that's an example. But you'll want to run your own 1k samples.
[00:02:18] Tom Reyes: That 92% vs 98% is... that gap might be material for us. How would rollback work if we see regression in production?
[00:02:26] Alice Park: Good question. We have canary rollouts and an automatic fallback policy. If the monitor detects a drop in your configured metric — e.g., presence of hallucinated medication mentions — it'll route traffic back to the last known-good profile (usually FP8 or FP16). You can tune thresholds and window sizes.
[00:02:42] Angelica Moreno: What about tokenization differences — our EHR has lots of id weird strings, does the q-profile handle that?
[00:02:49] Marcus Li: Tokenization is deterministic per model; q-profiles don't change tokenization. But we do show token length distributions in the console so you can see where your workload sits relative to the benchmark.
[00:02:59] Dr. Priya Shah: Can we see the actual runs?
[00:03:02] Marcus Li: Sure, I'll switch to the bench tab. (30s pause) Okay I launched an A/B with 500 samples each from a sanitized sample set. You'll see three panes: latency histograms, top regressed prompts list, and quality delta table.
[00:03:22] [00:03:22] Marcus Li: For this run, int8-speed produced median latency 42ms, p95 78ms, cost/unit down 48%. FP8 had median 88ms, p95 140ms, cost down 20% relative to fp16. In quality delta, the top regressions were around rare medication disambiguation cases.
[00:03:45] Tom Reyes: Could the medication issue be fixed by prompt engineering or is it the quantization?
[00:03:51] Marcus Li: It can be both. Some prompts amplify sensitive tokens; for others, the quant noise can hurt low-frequency token weights. On console you can attach selective high-precision overrides for token spans or fall back for specific routes. It's called precision overlays.
[00:04:09] Angelica Moreno: Precision overlays — that sounds promising. Are those per-route or per-prompt?
[00:04:15] Alice Park: Per-route or per-caller. You can map critical flows to fp8 or fp16 while keeping the rest on int8 to save cost.
[00:04:24] Dr. Priya Shah: Walk me through the regression list — can I inspect examples?
[00:04:28] Marcus Li: Yep. (scrolls) Here's an example: reference: "Patient discharged w/ 5mg metoprolol qday"; fp8 preserves metoprolol correctly, int8 output changed to "metoprol" which is ambiguous. You can flag that prompt and add it to a failure set; we then surface it to the fallback rules.
[00:04:50] [00:05:00] Tom Reyes: What's the best practice for rollout length? How many requests for a canary?
[00:05:05] Marcus Li: We recommend 1-5% traffic for initial canary with at least 1k requests or a time window that covers your workload variance. For rare medical tokens you might need targeted canaries using the failure set.
[00:05:20] Angelica Moreno: Ours is bursty — weekdays peak at 10k/min for background summarization; user interactive is smaller but latency-sensitive.
[00:05:29] Alice Park: You can do route-level burst policies. Also Optimize suggests batching and cache settings; for interactive we suggest low batch sizes and small KV cache expiry, for background you can increase batch and cache.
[00:05:42] Dr. Priya Shah: On the security side, can you confirm no raw PHI leaves our VPC?
[00:05:49] Alice Park: For Private deployment, data never leaves the controlled network. Audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM, KMS integration supports customer-managed keys, and we support HSM in on-prem. I'll attach the Private deployment checklist.
[00:06:03] Tom Reyes: Great. Also, do you have SLA numbers for p95 latency?
[00:06:08] Marcus Li: Dedicated/reserved capacity tiers come with latency SLOs; hosted is best-effort. We'll send the SLA doc but typically dedicated pools give you p95 targets within Xms based on GPU class. We'll tailor for your committed capacity.
[00:06:23] Angelica Moreno: Can you show the cost delta per 1M tokens?
[00:06:28] Marcus Li: On the console cost panel — int8-speed estimated ~$0.12 per 1k tokens for this model in our sandbox, fp8 ~0.22 per 1k, fp16 ~0.45 per 1k. These numbers vary by hardware and reserved discounts.
[00:06:46] Dr. Priya Shah: Back to quality — you mentioned custom rubrics. How do we integrate our QA checks?
[00:06:52] Alice Park: You can upload CSVs of input, reference, and a JS scoring function or choose from built-in metrics. The Evaluate runner will compute per-sample scores and then we can configure alerts on aggregated metrics.
[00:07:05] Tom Reyes: If we find a significant regression in a metric, can the system auto-block a rollout?
[00:07:11] Marcus Li: Yes, there's a guardrail option. You set a threshold and a window; if crossed, traffic automatically reverts and an incident is created with the top failing prompts.
[00:07:22] Angelica Moreno: I want to make sure we capture edge cases — rare drug names, lab abbreviations. Can we seed the bench with targeted prompts?
[00:07:30] Marcus Li: Absolutely, you can upload a targeted sample set. Also the console supports weighting so those samples are overrepresented in the bench.
[00:07:40] Dr. Priya Shah: On pilot scope — what would a minimal pilot look like?
[00:07:44] Alice Park: Minimal pilot: you provide 1k de-identified samples, Redwood runs an int8/fp8 sweep and returns the CSV with per-sample diffs, console setup for canary and fallback rules, and a one-week canary in Private environment. We estimate 2-3 weeks end-to-end.
[00:07:59] Tom Reyes: Cost for pilot?
[00:08:02] Alice Park: Pilot is complimentary for qualified enterprise prospects; we just need the samples and an NDA if needed. Deployment engineering time for Private might be billable depending on scope.
[00:08:13] Angelica Moreno: Okay. Could you show the runbook for an automatic fallback?
[00:08:17] Marcus Li: Sure, here's the policy editor. (navigates) You can choose metric, comparator (drop > 3% accuracy), window, and action: rollback to previous profile, route 100% to FP8, or raise a pager. You can also chain actions.
[00:08:36] [00:08:50] Alice Park: One nuance — FP8 is often a middle ground; some customers prefer hybrid where embedding/encoder layers use higher precision. Optimize supports layer-level quant overrides but that's an advanced flow.
[00:09:02] Marcus Li: Also worth noting — INT8 gains are model-architecture-dependent. For some models INT8 is quite aggressive; for others it's near fp8. We recommend a sensitivity sweep.
[00:09:13] Dr. Priya Shah: Do you support mixed-precision per-token?
[00:09:17] Marcus Li: Not per-token; per-route or per-layer. Per-token would be complex at runtime.
[00:09:24] Angelica Moreno: Any red flags we should watch for during rollout?
[00:09:27] Marcus Li: Watch low-frequency token mispredictions, sudden drop in named-entity extraction scores, and user-reported hallucinations. The console will surface sudden deltas.
[00:09:39] Tom Reyes: How does this compare to Lambda/Anthropic offerings?
[00:09:44] Alice Park: Anthropic and Lambda have strong points — Anthropic around safety and spec compliance, Lambda around self-hosted stacks. We differentiate with unified Optimize tooling across Hosted/Dedicated/Private plus built-in rollback and eval integrations tailored for production RL workflows.
[00:09:59] Dr. Priya Shah: Are there any known medical domain regressions in your released q-profiles?
[00:10:05] Marcus Li: Most regressions are low-frequency token errors. For clinical content we advise a conservative default (fp8) and selective int8 where cost is critical. We'll run your data and share results.
[00:10:16] Angelica Moreno: Ok let's talk timeline and owners — I want the pilot ready before our next compliance review end of July.
[00:10:24] Alice Park: We'll target a pilot kickoff the week of July 27th. Marcus will run the sweep by 7/20 and Alice will send security docs by 7/17.
[00:10:34] [00:10:40] Alice Park: Any other questions?
[00:10:42] Tom Reyes: One last — if we need to audit why a particular inference changed, can we get token-level diffs?
[00:10:48] Marcus Li: We surface top-k token deltas and attention-map-ish summaries in the debug export, though attention maps aren't always precise; but yes you can get per-step deltas for an audited prompt.
[00:11:02] Dr. Priya Shah: That should help for root cause.
[00:11:05] Angelica Moreno: Cool. Next steps recap?
[00:11:08] Alice Park: Marcus run int8/fp8 sweep on samples after you deliver 1k set, Alice sends security+SOW, GammaHealth delivers samples. We'll schedule a 30 min kickoff to set up Private bench.
[00:11:19] Tom Reyes: Sounds good. Thanks both.
[00:11:23] Alice Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links to the deck and pilot instructions.
[00:11:27] End of meeting
